newsitem.title: GERMANY: German industry sees more job cuts, slower growth.
newsitem.headline: German industry sees more job cuts, slower growth.

text.p: As fresh evidence emerged that Germany's worst post-war jobs crisis continues unabated, leading industry groups disputed government economic forecasts and said on Thursday that companies were set to cut even more jobs.

Drawing on its latest survey of 25,000 companies, the Federation of Chambers of Industry and Commerce (DIHT) said every third business in Germany planned to cut jobs this year and more than a third would invest less than the year before.
"Our impression is that there is no willingness to invest more as the year begins," DIHT managing director Franz Schoser told a news conference.

The results of the annual survey of member businesses led DIHT to predict that the economy would probably stagnate in the first quarter of the year and that growth would be just two percent for the full year.

The German government stands by its forecast of 2.5 percent growth this year, despite a further climb in unemployment to a post-war record of nearly 4.7 million in February. The growth forecast underpins plans to cut borrowing this year in order to qualify for European monetary union (EMU).

The government's view appeared to gain weight as industry orders data released on Thursday showed an unexpected rise of 2.4 percent in January from the previous month and 4.6 percent from the year-earlier month. December orders fell 1.9 percent from November and were up 1.9 percent from a year ago.

Separately, Germany's capital equipment and plant construction industry said the job situation in the sector could improve in the second half of 1997 after a slight decline in staff numbers in the first half.

Overall, joblessness in the sector can be halved in the medium term, the VDMA association said in a statement. At the end of December the sector employed 942,000 people compared to 981,000 the year before.
DIHT said the economy was struggling to make progress. Exports would remain the main driver in 1997, thanks to global economic recovery and the depreciation of the German mark.
But the bad news for the labour market is that domestic growth remains weak, with investment and consumer demand weak and "gloomy" prospects for the important building sector.

Industry has pinned its hopes on talks between Chancellor Helmut Kohl's centre-right coalition and the opposition Social Democrats (SPD) that are aimed at reaching a compromise by Easter on huge tax cuts for businesses and individuals.

But the Federation of German Industry (BDI), the main industry lobby, said these plans were just the beginning of needed changes and that companies would continue to move jobs abroad as the world economy becomes more intertwined.

"Germany as a location for investment and production cuts an unsatisfactory figure not only in terms of labour costs but also in terms of the burden of taxes and charges," the BDI said in a summary of its annual report to be published next week.
"Even small and medium-sized companies are now using the proximity of the reforming states of central and eastern Europe for sub-contracting of manufacturing components."
Kohl's Christian Democrats (CDU) reacted angrily to the new round of industry demands for government action, saying it was time for business to play its part in fighting unemployment.
CDU general secretary Peter Hintze said the government had enacted legislation that gave small companies more flexible hiring regulations and that it was on the way to implementing deep tax cuts.
"These were demands made by the employers. Now we are calling on employers to do their part and create jobs," he said.
